name: Synthetic Portraiture
title: Synthetic Portraiture
answer: Synthetic portraiture is the making of human or human-like likenesses with generative image models, whether the subject is a real person, a composite, or a wholly invented face. It sits inside photography and hyper-realism because its central claim is photographic: skin, light, lens behaviour and the small asymmetries that make a face read as a person rather than a render. The work spans editorial and advertising imagery, concept art, character design, family and memorial commissions, and the studio practice of photographers who now build a likeness in software before or instead of a camera. It also covers the harder cases, such as restaging a sitter who cannot be photographed again, or producing a face that belongs to no one.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most work runs through hosted text-to-image and image-to-image services, with a smaller share on local installations of open models where a studio wants control over weights and data. The site currently tracks 1000 live image generation models, and the practical choice is usually between a general model that renders convincing skin and a fine-tuned or LoRA-adapted model trained on one face or one lighting style. A typical setup adds a diffusion or transformer-based generator, an upscaler, a face restoration or detail pass, and a control layer such as pose, depth or reference image conditioning. Output is judged on a colour-managed display, then finished in ordinary retouching software, so the pipeline is closer to a digital darkroom than to a single button.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The portrait is built in passes rather than in one prompt. A practitioner starts with a reference, either a photograph of the sitter or a generated face, then fixes pose, framing and lighting with conditioning inputs before letting the model resolve texture and expression. Iteration is the craft: many low-cost variations, selection by eye, then inpainting to correct hands, ears, hairline and the catchlight in the eye, which are the places where synthetic faces most often fail. Identity consistency across a set is handled with a trained adapter, a reference image, or a fixed seed and prompt structure, and the final frame is graded and retouched so it sits beside camera-made work without obvious seams. Documentation of the steps matters, because a client or an editor will ask how the image was made.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The rights questions are unsettled and vary by jurisdiction. Likeness, personality and publicity rights sit with the person depicted, and a synthetic face that resembles a real, identifiable individual can raise claims even when no photograph was used. Copyright in a purely generated image is uncertain in several countries, and training data provenance is the subject of active litigation, part of the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits the site tracks. Practical studios keep model and version records, prompt and seed logs, consent or licence paperwork for any real sitter, and a clear label when an image is synthetic, especially in journalism, advertising and anything that could be mistaken for documentary evidence. Nothing here is legal advice, and the rules differ by market and by client.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect identity control to keep improving, so a consistent face can be carried across many images, angles and even video with less manual repair. Detection and provenance marking are advancing alongside generation, which pushes studios toward documented, labelled workflows rather than undetectable output. The likely split is between commercial work that treats synthetic likeness as a normal production tool and editorial or documentary work that reserves photography for images made with a camera. Consent, licensing and disclosure practice will probably settle faster than copyright, because clients and platforms can set their own terms. The craft question stays the same: whether the face reads as a person, and whether the maker can say honestly how it was made.
